hook: Myth: everyone noticed that embarrassing thing you did.

blocks.narration: Myth: everyone noticed that embarrassing thing you did. Fact: far fewer people noticed than you think. Psychologists can prove it.
blocks.visual: Minimal surreal 3D clay figure under a huge harsh spotlight while other clay figures look elsewhere, pastel light

blocks.narration: In a study published in two thousand, psychologist Thomas Gilovich asked students to wear an embarrassing T-shirt into a room of peers.
blocks.visual: A clay student nervously walks through a door wearing a loud cartoon T-shirt

blocks.narration: The shirt featured a singer most students found deeply uncool. The wearers were then asked how many people noticed it.
blocks.visual: Clay classmates sit at desks, mostly busy with their own notebooks

blocks.narration: They guessed that about half the room noticed. In reality, only about a quarter of the people in the room actually did.
blocks.visual: Two pie charts side by side, the predicted one half full, the real one only a quarter

blocks.narration: This is called the spotlight effect. We consistently overestimate how much other people notice our appearance, mistakes, and awkward moments.
blocks.visual: The giant spotlight shrinks to a tiny flashlight beam

blocks.narration: It happens because you live inside your own head all day. Everyone else is busy starring in their own story.
blocks.visual: Every clay figure in the room now has their own tiny spotlight, each focused on themselves

blocks.narration: That stumble, that typo, that bad hair day. Most people barely registered it, and almost nobody remembers it tomorrow.
blocks.visual: Small clay thought bubbles pop and vanish above the classmates

blocks.narration: Knowing this can make you bolder in everyday life, so go try the thing. Send this to a friend who overthinks everything.
blocks.visual: The clay student smiles and steps forward confidently as the camera pulls back

cta: Send this to a friend who overthinks everything.

captions.hook_line: People notice your embarrassing moments far less than you think 👀
captions.body: In a 2000 study by Thomas Gilovich and colleagues, students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about half of their peers noticed it; only about a quarter actually did. This is called the spotlight effect.

youtube_title: Nobody Is Noticing You as Much as You Think
